name: Priya Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at six, I do twenty minutes of prayer and stretching, then I work on my plan at the kitchen table. I'm building a home admin and bookkeeping service for small shops, with an AI assistant doing the first drafts. In the afternoon I knock on doors in Rivermouth, handing out cards. Until August I was the office administrator at Pellam and Sons Insurance Brokers, seven years. Mr Pellam retired, the buyer moved everything online, and my job went with the filing cabinets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it's mostly hype, that's fine by me, because I've been using these tools every day and I know what they can and can't do. They save time, but they don't build a business. That still takes a person who knocks on doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say these tools are helpful and over-sold. I'd tell my cousins in the family business to use them for the dull jobs, like invoices and emails, and to keep the customers personal. I'd also say people should work for their own living and not wait for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried about AI as much as I'm worried about cash. I've no savings, the benefits just cover rent and food, and starting a business with nothing in the bank is nerve-racking. My mother keeps saying I should find a steady job and then think about settling down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building my admin service: sign up five shops by Christmas at about eighty pounds a month each, and use AI to turn their messy receipts into tidy books. I'd also apply for part-time office jobs as a safety net. I'd ask the chamber of commerce for a free stall at their small business morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and tense, like walking a tightrope in good weather. I like the work, but every pound I spend on cards and printing feels big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you plan to win those first five shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being local and by being reliable. I know the owner of the dry cleaner's and the florist, Mrs Gill, because I used to arrange their insurance. I'd offer a free first month, and show them how much time they save, using their own paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mother mean about settling down, and does it affect your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd like me married with a family before I'm thirty-six, and I'd like that too, someday. It affects my plan because I want to earn a steady income before I bring anyone into my life. I don't want to be a burden, and I don't want to start a family on benefits.

say: I'd say these tools are **helpful and over-sold**, and good for invoices and emails.
I'd say people should **own living** and not wait for anyone.
think: My worry is **cash**, because benefits just cover rent and food.
My mother says I should find a **steady job** and then settle down.
do: Sign up **five shops** by Christmas at about eighty pounds a month each.
Apply for **part-time office jobs** as a safety net.
Ask the chamber of commerce for a free **stall** at their small business morning.
feel: Hopeful and tense, like a **tightrope** in good weather.
S0.quote: I don't want to be a burden, and I don't want to start a family on benefits.
fieldNote: Ties her **business plan** to her family plans in a clear order.
Uses AI as a **first draft** tool, never as a replacement for door knocking.
Anxious because the income is zero and each printing cost feels big.

steps.text: Sign up five local shops for monthly bookkeeping by Christmas
Apply for part-time office jobs as a safety net
Ask the chamber of commerce for a free stall at its business morning
Use an AI assistant to turn messy receipts into tidy books

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one that hit my old job, I think. Booking, checking, planning, answering customers is what an insurance office does all day. It's what the new owner did with software at Pellam and Sons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for the quick and the careful. People who run the tools can do the work of three. I'd also say we should keep family firms alive, because they treat people with respect, and that the government shouldn't drown small business in rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my service might be exactly what small shops need, because they can't afford the software teams and don't have time to learn. But I can see big firms offering the same cheaply. My edge is trust and being a face people know. That's something a screen can't sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up a package for small shops: bookkeeping, invoices, appointment reminders and customer replies, all done with AI behind the scenes and me checking. I'd ask three early customers to write a short review. I'd take an online accounting software course, and join the local small-business association for contacts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a little frightened. I feel like I've seen the wave and I'm learning to surf, but my board is borrowed and my pockets are empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you stop big firms from undercutting you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By doing what they can't, which is turning up. I'd go in, sit down with the owner and know their business, their quirks, even their children's names. A cheap app doesn't ring on a Monday morning to ask how the weekend was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your cousins in the family business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To use the tools to answer customers faster, but to keep one person for the human calls. My uncle has run his shop for thirty years and he says people come back for him, not the till. I'd tell them that's worth protecting.

say: I'd say this is a chance for the **quick and careful**, since people running the tools do the work of three.
I'd say governments shouldn't drown **small business** in rules.
think: Small shops need what I offer, but big firms may sell it **cheaply** too.
My edge is **trust** and being a face people know.
do: Offer a package of **bookkeeping, reminders and replies**, with AI behind the scenes and me checking.
Ask three early customers for short **reviews**.
Take an online **accounting software** course and join the small-business association.
feel: Excited and frightened, learning to surf on a **borrowed board** with empty pockets.
S1.quote: A cheap app doesn't ring on a Monday morning to ask how the weekend was.
fieldNote: Sees **trust and presence** as her edge over cheap software.
Wants to protect **family firms**, in line with her traditional outlook.
Anxious because her first customers are not yet signed.

steps.text: Offer small shops a bookkeeping and reminder package with AI checked by me
Use an AI assistant to draft client invoices and replies, then check each one
Take an online accounting software course
Join the local small-business association for contacts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd say that's a shock, but I've always been the one who prepares early, so I'd start the same day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities must prepare now, because governments will be slow. I'd tell people to save, learn the tools and stay close to their own. And I'd say no one should be left to face it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd have to move very fast to build an income before the market floods with people like me. Everyone who loses a desk job will try to start a one-person business. I'd have maybe a year of an advantage as an early mover, and then the crowd arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign as many small shops as I could in six months, even at low prices, so I'd have a base of regulars. I'd also learn a second skill that needs a person present, like care-home administration or event help, to cover the years when robots come. I'd ask my parents if I could move in for a while to save on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense and wide awake. I'd be thinking about family a lot, and whether I should be hurrying plans. It feels like trying to catch a bus that's already pulling away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the family plans with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably bring the conversation forward with my parents. I'd still want a stable income first, but I'd stop waiting for the perfect moment. If a good match came along, I'd rather build together than struggle alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your fallback if the shops don't sign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part-time admin at a care home or a school, which still need a human face for a few years. It pays less, but it's steady. And I'd keep the business as a side line until the crowd thins out.

say: I'd say families and communities must **prepare now**, because governments will be slow.
I'd say no one should face it **alone**.
think: I'd need to build income quickly **before the crowd** of other one-person businesses arrives.
I'd have maybe a year as an **early mover**.
do: Sign as many small shops as I could in **six months**, even at low prices.
Learn a second skill needing a person present, like **care-home administration**.
Ask my parents if I could **move in** for a while to save on rent.
feel: Tense and wide awake, like catching a **bus** already pulling away.
S2.quote: Everyone who loses a desk job will try to start a one-person business.
fieldNote: Spots the **crowd problem** for her own plan, which is sharp.
Brings **family plans forward**, since traditional values matter to her.
Alarmed because her advantage might last about a year.

steps.text: Sign as many small shops as possible within six months at low starter prices
Take a care-home administration course for a second income
Move in with my parents to save on rent
Talk with my parents about bringing family plans forward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a decent stretch. It's still fast, but long enough to build something if I begin now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for families to prepare, if they save and learn together. I'd say schools should bring back real apprenticeships. And I'd say hard work and community will count for more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I could build a steady little business in that time, with ten or fifteen regular clients, and then a second service on top as the tools improve. By 2031 plenty of office work will be done by machines, so being the human who looks after them is my niche. I'd feel proud of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the client list during the first year, then add a part-time degree in accounting. I'd save at least two months' rent by the end of year two. I'd also pick someone to train, perhaps my younger cousin, to take on simple jobs, so the business doesn't depend on me alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly hopeful. It's like preparing a long trip with a good map, even though I haven't packed my bag yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd be hurrying, with no time to fix mistakes. With five years I can try things, get them wrong, and still recover. That room for mistakes is what makes it a plan and not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the hardest bit of that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first year with almost no income. If I can't pay the rent, I'd have to take a job and lose time for the business. I'd lean on my parents for a loan if it came to it, though I'd hate to ask.

say: I'd say five years is long enough for families to **prepare** if they save and learn together.
I'd say schools should bring back real **apprenticeships**.
think: I could build a steady business with **ten or fifteen regulars**, then add a second service.
Being the **human** who looks after the machines is my niche.
do: Build the **client list** in year one, then add a part-time accounting degree.
Save at least **two months'** rent by the end of year two.
Train my younger **cousin** to take on simple jobs.
feel: Fairly hopeful, like a long trip with a **good map** but an unpacked bag.
S3.quote: With five years I can try things, get them wrong, and still recover. That room for mistakes is what makes it a plan and not a scramble.
fieldNote: Values **room for mistakes** as the key difference from a short deadline.
Plans to **train a cousin**, tying work to family.
Names the first income-free year as the main risk.

steps.text: Build a list of ten to fifteen regular small-shop clients
Start a part-time accounting degree in year two
Save two months of rent by the end of year two
Train my younger cousin to handle simple client jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a full chapter of life. I'd be forty-four, maybe with a family, and with a business that has history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good time to rebuild how we live, with family and community at the centre, honest work rewarded and training that's real. I'd say it's a chance to get things right, if we don't waste it on slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years makes me quite optimistic about myself. I'd build the business, have a family, and keep learning the tools as they change. My worry is whether the gains stay in a few big firms and the rest of us end up working harder for less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the bookkeeping service into a small firm with two or three staff, take the accounting degree part-time, and save steadily. I'd marry and plan a family, with a house in the area I know. I'd also keep an AI tool as my daily assistant, so I'm always a step ahead of the next change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm and quietly confident, though not today's bank balance. Ten years feels like enough to be patient and get it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in year one with ten years in hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't chase every shop. I'd choose the ones that pay on time and want a long relationship, and build slowly. I'd learn the accounting rules properly first, so I never get a client into trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your family fit into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents would be around, helping with children, and my cousins would be part of the firm. I'd like a business that could be handed down, so my own children have something solid. It's an old-fashioned dream, but I like it.

say: I'd say ten years is a good time to rebuild with **family and community** at the centre.
I'd say it's a chance to get it right if we don't waste it on **slogans**.
think: Ten years makes me **optimistic**: build the business, have a family, keep learning.
I worry the **gains** stay in a few big firms.
do: Grow the service into a small firm with **two or three staff**.
Take the accounting degree **part-time** and save steadily.
Marry, plan a **family**, and buy a house nearby.
feel: Mostly calm and quietly confident, though **not about** today's bank balance.
S4.quote: I'd like a business that could be handed down, so my own children have something solid.
fieldNote: Wants a business that can be **handed down**, an old-fashioned dream.
Chooses **long relationships** over chasing every shop.
Anxious today since income is still zero, but confident long term.

steps.text: Grow the bookkeeping service into a small firm with two or three staff
Finish a part-time accounting degree
Marry and plan a family with a house near my parents
Save steadily every month from the first client payments

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Two years is too little to build an income, and I'd be racing a crowd of other people who just lost desk jobs, with nothing in the bank. What would help is a small start-up grant, quick training in the tools, and family and community standing behind people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being traditional and being modern aren't opposites. I use AI every day and I still want a family, a faith and a quiet business with my name on it. Please don't write people like me as old-fashioned or as reckless.

headlineQuote: Being traditional and being modern aren't opposites. I use AI every day and I still want a family, a faith and a quiet business with my name on it.
portrait: Priya is **34**, lives alone in Rivermouth, and has been on **benefits only** since an insurance brokerage's office job ended in August.
She spent seven years as office administrator, now builds a **bookkeeping service** for small shops with AI first drafts.
She uses AI daily, but says her edge is **trust and turning up**.
She leans traditional: work over handouts, family firms, and settling down once she has **steady income**.
She is anxious in most scenarios and **alarmed** at two years, fearing a crowd of new one-person businesses.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to build income before a crowd of others arrives.
whatWouldHelp: A **small start-up grant** and quick training in the tools.
